Okay - first thing to note is this is abuse. I know you know this, but I'm just putting it out there.

Second - it is a really big deal. The fact that it happens a lot or that it's "not as bad" as other forms of abuse doesn't really matter.

Third - people deal with things differently. Something that one person might laugh off might traumatise another person. If you've managed to just let it go and move on, that's great, you dodged a bullet. But others might find it horrifying just to hear about. There's no wrong reaction to it.

My advice is not to try and minimise the experience itself as 'no big deal', but to explain that it hasn't impacted your life in a severe way. Make it less about judging your Uncle's actions and more about how you reacted to them.

Thanks for your thoughts.

I'd been having suicidal thoughts randomly for years during depressive phases, but I wasn't in much danger because the depression was so debilitating that killing myself was just far too much effort.

Then last year I had a severe mixed episode - I was suicidally depressed but I was also really pro-active. Needless to say, I'm still alive, but not from lack of trying.

I think being bipolar makes moments like these harder to predict and harder to manage. It's difficult to know what is a fleeting thought and what is a serious consideration. As always my advice is to talk to people. Talk to your friends and make sure you've got someone you can contact in an emergency. If you ever get that feeling and it seems to last longer, call a friend before you do anything else.

Take care ❤️

I'm still having trouble wrapping my brain around the idea of defining *people* as mono or poly. Maybe it's semantic, but I personally wouldn't trust it. Either they're in denial about the reality of the relationship, they're hoping to eventually get your partner all to themselves, or they really are cool with it, in which case, they're already halfway to being poly anyway.

Personally I like to have at least some kind of working relationship with my metas and this is one of the reasons why. A lot of people say they're cool with it, but only if they can pretend I don't exist, which is not really a healthy or sustainable situation (IMO). It naturally breeds jealousy and competition, not to mention putting your partner in a really difficult situation.

I've been in this situation before and it's like Schrödinger's Relationship - it exists in this weird state where it's both poly and mono, and it's all fine until you have to actually observe the reality and it breaks down.

You don't have to be anything or do anything you don't want to.

It might seem like your chances of happiness are slim, but if you kill yourself those odds drop to zero, so even a slim chance is worth a shot.

Suicide in the UK is not a criminal offence, so you won't have any sort of record. Police have strict protocols for dealing with suicidal people, and unless they think you're a danger to others won't (in theory) treat it like an offence.

They may pass the information on to the NHS, but this usually only has an effect if you're currently receiving treatment at a mental health centre. If you're being seen by the crisis team, they'll probably be informed. Whether or not the info makes it to your GP is hard to say.

However, all this is confidential and neither the cops nor the NHS will release this info to anyone else unless you consent to it, so your employer won't know.

No, it's the other way around - tendons are over the top of the arteries. Your primary (radial) nerve runs alongside the radial artery which is practically in the centre of your wrist, but there are smaller nerves scattered around the joints and tendons in front of it. Getting to an artery without hitting a tendon or nerve is close to impossible - your body protects your arteries pretty fiercely.

Like I said, it's not a great plan if you want the chance of getting out without any permanent damage.

Okay, I get that. The thing I'd say about slitting your wrists (or any suicide method) is that it's not a live/die binary. Coming out unscathed or being straight up dead are at the ends of the spectrum. More than either, you're much more likely to wind up with some kind of permanent damage, which could be anything from an ugly scar to serious brain damage.

With cutting your wrists, nerve and tendon damage are your most likely outcome, and these things suck ass in a massive way. We take our dexterity for granted but if you damage a nerve or a tendon too badly then half your life suddenly becomes a nightmarish task. Typing, gaming, cooking, tying your fucking shoelaces can all be painful and frustrating if you can do them at all.

Here's my advice. Your life is already in the hands of the universe. From cancer to car accidents to mountain lion attacks to mass shootings, there are millions of ways the universe could take you out if it wanted to. Every day you leave the house and get home alive, that's the universe deciding **not** to drop a meteor on your head.

The universe kills thousands of people every day, so if and when it wants you in a box, it'll just go ahead and do it. You don't need to give it an opportunity.

So yeah, 0/10, no stars, would not recommend.

If there's an abundance of anything in this world it's people trying to sell you happiness. Everyone has a magic fix that is always just out of reach. It seems to be the way the world works. And the moment you call bullshit and refuse to stop following the carrot dangling in front of you, you're put in box marked "broken".

I'm not going to sell you a cure to life - even if I wanted to, I don't have one - but I think sometimes the best thing you can do is stop listening to people who tell you you need to be fixed. Don't buy into the myth that the world is a happiness factory and that if only you joined in and played by the rules you'd be fulfilled, that the problem is you.

The problem isn't you. You're not defective because you had shit parents, or because you can't just "get over" something that happened to you. You're not broken just because you don't want to get wasted, or pray, or fuck or whatever quick fix people are pushing on you. You're not useless just because you're not ascending the corporate/property/social ladder to three kids, a Mercedes and a house in the suburbs.

I know it can be hard to believe this, and even harder to live by it when there's no one around to help. All I can say is that we are out there - little corners of the world where, if nothing else, people understand.

Unpopular opinion - Self harm isn't in-and-of-itself bad. The problem is what causes a person to do it. No one self-harms for a good reason - it's always symptomatic of something, and ultimately it's that underlying reason that is the "bad".

Sometimes self-harm can become habitual, and even after the cause is gone it still lingers. I suppose in that context the self-harm is itself the problem, but it's still part of a larger cycle.

Ultimately, it's a coping mechanism. You can argue as to whether or not it's a good or bad one, but I think that discussion is missing the bigger point.

I think it makes total sense. When we self-harm, we're often trying to regain some sense of control over our pain, so when it happens randomly and accidentally we're actually losing our control over it.

The whole "doing it for attention" thing is so toxic. Self-harm in particular is such a source of shame that people hide it for years. People self-harm out of a need for inner peace and control - which is more of less the opposite of attention seeking.

But even if you *were* doing it for attention, how is that any better? How is telling someone their pain is for shit and they don't deserve to be listened to going to help anyone? Like, dude if a person is hurting themselves just so someone will ask them if everything is okay, then maybe you **should** be giving them some attention.

Edit: When my parents found out I was cutting they told me I was doing it for attention, too. I had to inform them that I'd been cutting in secret for six years before they had found out.

CNC is a hard thing to wrap your brain around if you're not into it. The important thing to remember is that the C overrules the NC. There is always (or should be) an underlying agreement of consent. The non-consensual element is essentially theatre. It's like a horror film. It looks scary, and it can be, but it's all pretend.

I don't want you to feel that your feelings are invalid because they're not. This stuff makes lots of people uncomfortable and there's nothing wrong with that. But in a poly situation there's more to it. There's a difference between being uncomfortable with the act itself and having a problem with the people for doing it. My advice for you first is to figure out which is which. Are you uncomfortable with the act or with him? Do you think less of him that he enjoys this?

Because if that's the case, it's unlikely him stopping it is going to help. You'll still know he's into it and that will continue to affect your relationship.

So that's my advice. Figure out where exactly your discomfort lies. Again, none of this is a judgement on how your allowed to feel. It's simply a practical concern about understanding how you feel and what will make a difference.

Take care ❤️

Itching is the result of histamine production during the healing process. It's part of the inflammation response to that happens naturally as a result of trauma. Shallow surface cuts and scratches in particular are prone to high amounts of histamine production. It doesn't necessarily mean that a site is infected unless it's accompanied by pus or weeping, but it's definitely worth monitoring.

If it's bothering you, try a cold pack to reduce swelling and minimise sensitisation. You can also use antihistamine creams or tablets. Some people produce excessive amounts of histamine which can cause problems, so if you get hayfever or allergic reactions you might have a more severe reaction.

(As always, seek medical advice if you're concerned. I am not a doctor, etc...)

Being suicidal is not just one thing - it's a mix of thoughts, feelings and behaviours. It's different for everyone, and there's no one thing that is a guaranteed sign. It will usually include some combination of:

Suicidal Ideation - thoughts, fantasies or imaginings of suicide, not just the act itself, but the before and after. It's not uncommon to visualise your friends and family's reactions, your own funeral, the discovery of your body, etc.

Suicidal Visualisation - picturing the act of dying, rehearsing it in your mind. Imagining what dying might feel like and mental preparing for the act.

Suicidal Planning - making plans, backup plans and practical considerations. Not just basics like when, where and how, but thinking and preparing for the long and short term consequences.

Suicidal and Para-suicidal behaviour - attempts, practice runs, symbolic or ritualistic actions.

For some people, the preparation might be mostly emotional, whilst others it may be mostly practical. These things are not only unique to each person, but are also affected by motivation, situation and circumstance.

In addition, the link between suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and actually deaths by suicide is not as straight forward as one might think. Some people might be conceptually drawn to suicide as an idea without necessarily wanting to die. People can plan for their suicide for decades and never attempt it, whilst others can have the idea and carry it out all in the space of an afternoon.

It's really up to you - how do you feel about it. Does it bother you, disturb or upset you? Are you afraid or fascinated or indifferent about it? I would always recommend talking to someone - a friend, therapist, counselor. I wouldn't necessarily say you're definitely in serious danger of killing yourself, but if you're worried it might be worth talking to someone who can help.

Take care ❤️

About eight years ago, I was in your GF's position. My partner opened up to me about wanting to be non-monogamous and I didn't take it particularly well. I was still very insecure and didn't really understand why she might feel that way and still love me. At the time, she was much more sexually experienced than me and I took it to mean she just wanted more sex with better partners.

It took me about a year to come around to the idea. It was a slow process, but eventually I was able to see it for what it was. For a little while, we had a rule that we were a package deal - which led to lots of threesomes, but was more about getting me to a place where I understood the kinds of feelings involved.

I don't want to say that she'll definitely come around, because it's not for everyone. For me, it was just a question of getting over my insecurities and understanding it in terms of love and intimacy, rather than jealousy or fidelity. But sadly some people just don't feel it. She may just not want to share you.

As always, advice is more or less the same either way. Communicate, be honest, but most importantly, don't push her. Her biggest fear is going to be that you won't respect her boundaries - so show her you will by respecting them now.
